title: Business Law Basics
summary: Learn the legal essentials of running a business: choosing a structure and limited liability, registration and compliance, VAT and other taxes, employment and consumer law, intellectual property, data protection and resolving disputes.
audience: Entrepreneurs, managers, business students and freelancers

body.p: The legal form of a business decides who owns it, who is liable for its debts, how it is taxed and how easily it can raise money. Names and details differ between countries, but the main forms are similar.

list: Sole proprietor (sole trader): one owner, easy and cheap to start, but the owner is personally liable for all business debts.
Partnership: two or more owners sharing profits and, usually, unlimited liability for debts. A written partnership agreement is essential.
Private limited company: a separate legal person owned by shareholders, whose liability is limited to what they invested. More paperwork and reporting.
Public company: can offer shares to the public, with strict disclosure rules.
Cooperatives and non-profit companies: for member-owned or social purposes.

body.p: Suppose a business fails owing R500 000 with assets worth R200 000. A sole trader may have to pay the R300 000 shortfall from personal savings, house or car. If the business is a limited company and the owner invested R50 000 in shares, the owner normally loses that investment but not personal assets, unless they gave personal guarantees or acted fraudulently or recklessly.

body.tip: Banks often ask company directors for personal guarantees on loans. Read them carefully: they remove the protection of limited liability for that debt.

body.p: Most businesses must register their name or company with a national registry, such as the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) in Nigeria, the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC) in South Africa, the Business Registration Service in Kenya and the Office of the Registrar of Companies in Ghana. Many registrations are now online.

list: File annual returns and keep registry details up to date.
Register for income tax and, above the threshold, for value-added tax (VAT).
Keep proper accounting records for the period the law requires.
Obtain licences and permits for regulated activities, such as food, health, transport or financial services.
Register employees for payroll taxes and social security or pension schemes where required.
Hold meetings and keep minutes as company law requires.

body.p: Missing deadlines can bring penalties, interest and, eventually, deregistration. A simple compliance calendar listing every due date avoids most problems.

body.tip: Keep company documents (registration certificate, shareholder register, minutes, tax numbers) together in one secure folder, with digital copies.

body.p: Businesses pay taxes on profits and often collect taxes on behalf of the government. Rates and thresholds change, so always check the current rules with your tax authority or an accountant.

VAT is charged on sales and passed to the tax authority, minus the VAT the business paid on its own purchases. Standard rates differ: for example 15% in South Africa, 16% in Kenya and 7.5% in Nigeria at the time of writing. On a R1000 sale at 15%, VAT is R150, so the customer pays R1150. Working backwards from a VAT-inclusive price of R1150, the VAT is 1150 x 15 / 115 = R150.

list: Company income tax on profits, or personal income tax for sole traders and partners.
Pay-as-you-earn (PAYE): income tax deducted from employees' salaries and paid over by the employer.
Withholding taxes on certain payments, such as dividends or contractor fees in some countries.
Customs and excise duties on imports and some goods.
Local business levies and permits.

body.tip: Put aside the VAT and PAYE you collect in a separate account; it is the government's money, and spending it is a common cause of business failure.

body.p: Employment laws protect workers and set duties for employers. Examples include South Africa's Basic Conditions of Employment Act and Labour Relations Act, Nigeria's Labour Act and Kenya's Employment Act. Details differ, but common rules include:

list: Written terms or contracts of employment.
Minimum wages and limits on working hours, with overtime rules.
Paid annual leave, sick leave and maternity leave.
Fair reasons and fair procedures for discipline and dismissal.
Safe workplaces and protection from discrimination and harassment.
The right to join trade unions.

body.p: Consumer laws, such as South Africa's Consumer Protection Act, Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act and Kenya's Consumer Protection Act, require honest information, fair contract terms, safe goods, and remedies such as repair, replacement or refund for defective products. Misleading advertising and hidden charges are prohibited.

body.tip: Write clear returns and refund policies that at least match the legal minimum, and train staff to follow them.

body.p: Intellectual property (IP) protects creations of the mind. It can be one of a business's most valuable assets.

list: Trademarks protect brand names, logos and slogans that identify goods or services. Registering them gives stronger, easier-to-enforce rights.
Copyright protects original works such as writing, music, photographs, software code and designs. It arises automatically when the work is created, in most countries.
Patents protect new, inventive and useful inventions for a limited time, in exchange for publishing how they work.
Industrial designs protect the appearance of products.
Trade secrets, such as recipes or customer lists, are protected by keeping them confidential, often with non-disclosure agreements.
Search existing trademarks before choosing a name, to avoid infringing someone else's.
Make sure contracts with freelancers and staff say who owns the work they create.
Do not copy images, music or text from the internet without permission or a licence.
Regional systems such as ARIPO and OAPI can help protect IP across several African countries.

body.tip: Register your main brand name early in every country where you plan to trade.

body.p: Businesses that collect personal information, such as customer names, phone numbers, ID numbers or health data, must follow data-protection laws: POPIA in South Africa, the Nigeria Data Protection Act, Kenya's Data Protection Act, Ghana's Data Protection Act and GDPR for European customers.

list: Collect only what you need, for a clear and lawful purpose.
Tell people what you collect and why, and get consent where required.
Keep data secure and limit access.
Report serious breaches as the law requires.
Respect people's rights to see, correct and delete their data.

body.p: Put important agreements in writing: supplier contracts, customer terms, shareholder and partnership agreements, leases and employment contracts. When disputes arise, try negotiation first, then mediation (a neutral person helps both sides agree) or arbitration (a private decision-maker gives a binding decision), which are usually faster and cheaper than court. Small-claims courts handle low-value disputes simply in many countries.

body.tip: This course is general information, not legal advice. For important decisions, consult a qualified lawyer or accountant in your country.
